searchText: I was originally told not to rely on typed transaction type 0 to refer to legacy transactions, but it appears the JSON-RPC is using type 0 for I typed transactions. Is that bow a safe assumption? The 0 is reserved and used for legacy transactions? What endpoint is setting type to 0 for legacy transactions? 0 is *not* reserved for legacy transactions in any specification. GetTransactionReceipt 0x0 You are seeing this in production, or in the JSON-RPC spec? Production. INFURA, Etherscan. 😖 This is why we can't have nice things. I’ve only tested homestead. But have no reason to suspect any different on other networks. I could try the others. 1. we'll ask them to stop 2. they'll tell us "it makes things easier for our users" 3. we'll tell them but your users are going to break in a horrible way when we add a type 0 transaction type 4. they'll tell us that they'll deal with that when the time comes 5. we'll proceed to waste hundreds of engineering hours arguing over whether it is acceptable to break those users sometime in the future when we go to add a type 0 transaction It’s Geth and Parity (or whatever it’s called now). I suspect the conversation will go as above no matter who the culprit is. 😢 Though, depending on the culprit, avoiding future pain may sit better with some than others. <@543900561460822016> Do you happen to know which client is putting `0` for the transaction type of legacy transactions? I mean, we could also just reserve type 0 (along with 0x19). That still gives us like 126 types? And eth2 will use a different format, so that should be enough types for the next bit, no? 🙂 Well. To be honest, type 0 would make my life easier. Although, my life would be equally useful is -1 was used. But a number would be nice. You mean you want a discriminated union? ```ts type Transaction = { type: 0, ... } | { type: 1, ... } ``` I can appreciate how that might be marginally easier than: ```ts type Transaction = { type: never, ... } | { type: 1, ... } ``` geth uses 0 for legacy txs internally https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/5228b2a353726c7b163a534f5145e2f554c497dc/core/types/transaction.go#L45 Oh, more that the return type is `number` instead of `number | null` everywhere, which also means all consumers have to use `(tx.type == null) thingA: tx.type`. ```ts switch (transaction.type) { ... } ``` vs ```ts if ('type' in transaction) { ... } else switch (transaction.type) { ... } ``` I think I can be convinced to "reserve" a type for legacy transactions just from a usability standpoint. i guess the rpc is not omitting it for legacy txs? a: Record<number, Thing> = …; return a[tx.type] is nice and easy. Null checks are just unpleasant for everything. Especially if we can easily have a canonical value in the same type. 0xff is fine too. But something. 🙂 I can just make type 0 become type -1. But I’d rather not deviate too far if it is just going to be accepted as the canonical value, then some things will use 0 and ethers -1. Don't do negatives. The Ethereum protocol goes to great lengths to avoid negative numbers, they cause a ton of interoperability problems. Well they get converted before they hit the network. I already use -1 in serializeTransaction to be explicit to use legacy. Because there needs to be *a* number. tx = { type: null, value: 100 } should not be treated critically different, and generate completely different output from: tx = { type: undefined, value: 100 } Keep in mind ethers is largely porcelain, so negative numbers are isolated. But I would prefer 0. 🙂 IMO you shouldn't be using `number` in ethers (as I believe I have expressed before). 😁 Yes, but that change cannot be made in v5. And a major version change isn’t ready yet. If you are passionate about this and have the time, I think the best way to get `0` as reserved is to create the doc I mentioned in <#779922457631916064>. It is on my todo list, but far enough down that it will probably never actually get done. (I’m working on it though, and am quite excited for it. :)) If we had that list, we would have a place to reserve values, which would let us reserve 0. Yeah. My todo list still has 3 EIPs to update. :p Where does this list need to live? eth1.0-specs seems ideal. Ok. I just check out the repo and make a PR? I’m pretty passionate that 0x19 gets reserved. 🙂 Make a new folder in the root? I can get that together. I'm not sure, that is part of the challenge. 😬 <@552133098075193354> would be a good person to talk to about getting a place for a living document that tracks reserved secp256k1 signature prefixes. I'm pretty confident that eth1.0-specs is the right place, but I'm not sure *within* that where to put it. Maybe just create a folder called "lists" and put it in there? 😁 Ok. 🙂 I’ll ping him in a PR. 🙂 0, 1, leading legacy transaction bytes (I forget what they are, but it is a pretty constrained range), 19, and 3 should all be reserved I think. And 2. `[0,1,2,3,19,...valid_first_bytes_of_legacy_transaction]` <@358385024573243393> ☝️ What is 3? 0 = legacy transactions 1 = 2930 2 = 1559 3 = 3074 19 = signed message I’ve added 0, 1, 2 and 0x19 so far. Ok. I’ll look up and add 3 now. 🙂 https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3074
